description: What does a confusion matrix show?
explanation: It lays out predicted classes against actual classes, so you can see exactly which kinds of mistake are being made.
choice0: Predicted classes against actual classes, showing each kind of mistake
choice1: How confused the training process became
choice2: The correlation between every pair of features
choice3: How accuracy changed during training

description: What is a false positive?
explanation: A false positive is a case the model flagged as positive when it was actually negative.
choice0: A positive case the model missed
choice1: A negative case the model wrongly flagged as positive
choice2: A correct positive prediction
choice3: A case the model refused to classify

description: What is a false negative?
explanation: A false negative is a genuinely positive case that the model failed to flag.
choice0: A negative case wrongly flagged as positive
choice1: A correct negative prediction
choice2: A positive case the model missed
choice3: A prediction made with low confidence

description: What does precision measure?
explanation: Precision asks: of everything the model flagged as positive, what share really was positive?
hint: Precision looks at the predictions, recall looks at the real cases.
choice0: Of the cases flagged positive, how many really were
choice1: Of the real positive cases, how many were found
choice2: How close repeated predictions are to each other
choice3: The share of all predictions that were correct

description: What does recall measure?
explanation: Recall asks: of all the genuinely positive cases, what share did the model find?
choice0: Of the cases flagged positive, how many really were
choice1: How quickly the model returns a prediction
choice2: How often the model changes its mind
choice3: Of the real positive cases, how many the model found

description: For a cancer screening test, which error type is usually more costly?
explanation: A false negative sends a sick patient home untreated, which is generally far worse than the extra checks a false positive causes.
choice0: A false positive
choice1: A false negative
choice2: They are always equally costly
choice3: Neither, since accuracy covers both

description: For a spam filter, which error type usually annoys users most?
explanation: A false positive silently hides a real message, which is worse than a spam email slipping into the inbox.
choice0: A false positive, because a real message is hidden
choice1: A false negative, because spam reaches the inbox
choice2: Both are equally serious
choice3: Neither matters if accuracy is high

description: Why do precision and recall usually trade off against each other?
explanation: Flagging more cases catches more true positives but also more false ones, so raising recall tends to lower precision.
choice0: Because they measure the same thing differently
choice1: Because they are computed on different datasets
choice2: Because flagging more cases finds more true positives but also more false ones
choice3: Because precision applies to regression and recall to classification

description: What is the F1 score?
explanation: F1 combines precision and recall into a single number, and is low unless both are reasonably high.
choice0: A single score combining precision and recall
choice1: The accuracy of the first fold in cross-validation
choice2: The share of features that were useful
choice3: The error on the first training run

description: Which metric is appropriate for a regression model?
explanation: Regression errors are measured as distances, for example mean absolute error. Accuracy and recall apply to classification.
choice0: Accuracy
choice1: Recall
choice2: Precision
choice3: Mean absolute error

description: What does mean squared error penalise more heavily than mean absolute error?
explanation: Squaring makes large errors count disproportionately, so MSE is much more sensitive to big misses.
choice0: Small, frequent errors
choice1: Large individual errors
choice2: Errors on the training set only
choice3: Errors on rare classes

description: What is a validation set for?
explanation: A validation set is used while developing the model, to compare options and tune settings, keeping the test set untouched until the end.
choice0: Comparing options and tuning settings without touching the test set
choice1: Checking the data for missing values
choice2: Adding extra examples to training
choice3: Measuring how long training takes

description: What does k-fold cross-validation do?
explanation: It splits the data into k parts and trains k times, each time holding out a different part, then averages the results.
choice0: Trains k separate models and keeps the best one
choice1: Splits each feature into k ranges
choice2: Trains k times, holding out a different part each time, and averages the scores
choice3: Repeats training k times on the same split

description: Why is cross-validation useful on a small dataset?
explanation: Every example gets used for both training and evaluation across the folds, giving a more stable estimate than one small split.
choice0: It creates additional training examples
choice1: Every example is used for both training and evaluation, steadying the estimate
choice2: It removes the need for a test set entirely
choice3: It makes the model train faster

description: What is data leakage?
explanation: Leakage is when information that would not be available at prediction time reaches the model during training, inflating its scores.
choice0: Information unavailable at prediction time reaching the model during training
choice1: Training data being lost from storage
choice2: A model file being shared accidentally
choice3: Missing values spreading through a dataset

description: Why does scaling features using the whole dataset before splitting cause leakage?
explanation: The scaling absorbs information from the test rows, so the model has indirectly seen them.
choice0: It changes the labels
choice1: It makes the split uneven
choice2: The scaling carries information from the test rows into training
choice3: It removes outliers from the test set

description: A model predicting loan default has a feature called amount_recovered_after_default. What is wrong?
explanation: That value only exists after the outcome is known, so it leaks the answer and the model will fail in production.
choice0: It only exists after the outcome, so it leaks the answer
choice1: It is measured in the wrong units
choice2: It has too many missing values
choice3: It is correlated with another feature

description: Why does a model with suspiciously perfect test performance deserve scrutiny?
explanation: Near-perfect scores usually indicate leakage or a duplicated split rather than a genuinely excellent model.
choice0: Because perfect scores are impossible to compute
choice1: Because it usually signals leakage or overlapping train and test data
choice2: Because the test set must be too large
choice3: Because accuracy is not defined above 99 percent

description: What is feature engineering?
explanation: Feature engineering creates more useful inputs from the raw data, such as turning a birth date into an age.
choice0: Choosing which algorithm to use
choice1: Removing rows with missing values
choice2: Tuning the settings of the model
choice3: Creating more useful inputs from the raw data

description: Why is a raw timestamp often a poor feature on its own?
explanation: The useful signal is usually in derived parts such as hour of day or day of week, not the raw instant, which never repeats.
choice0: The signal usually lies in derived parts like hour or weekday, not the raw instant
choice1: Timestamps cannot be stored numerically
choice2: Timestamps always contain errors
choice3: Models cannot read dates at all

description: What does one-hot encoding do to a categorical column?
explanation: It replaces the category with one yes or no column per possible value, so no false ordering is implied.
choice0: Replaces categories with the numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on
choice1: Creates one yes or no column for each possible category
choice2: Removes the column if it has too many categories
choice3: Sorts the categories alphabetically

description: Why is labelling categories as 1, 2 and 3 risky for an unordered category like city?
explanation: Numbering implies an order and a spacing that do not exist, and some models will treat city 3 as greater than city 1.
choice0: It implies an order and spacing between cities that do not exist
choice1: It uses more memory than text
choice2: It prevents the column from being sorted
choice3: Models cannot handle integer columns

description: Why does feature scaling matter for distance-based methods such as k-nearest neighbours?
explanation: A feature measured in large units dominates the distance calculation, drowning out features on smaller scales.
choice0: Because unscaled features cannot be stored
choice1: Because scaling removes outliers
choice2: Because a large-scale feature dominates the distance and hides the others
choice3: Because distances must be whole numbers

description: What is the curse of dimensionality, informally?
explanation: As the number of features grows, the space becomes so sparse that examples are all far apart and patterns are harder to find.
choice0: Models refuse to run beyond a fixed number of columns
choice1: With many features the data becomes sparse and patterns get harder to find
choice2: Extra features always cause missing values
choice3: High-dimensional data cannot be visualised at all

description: Why can adding more features sometimes make a model worse?
explanation: Irrelevant or noisy features give the model more opportunity to fit coincidences, which hurts performance on new data.
choice0: Noisy or irrelevant features give the model more coincidences to fit
choice1: Extra features always slow prediction below a usable speed
choice2: Models can only handle ten features
choice3: Extra features remove the need for training data

description: What is an ensemble method?
explanation: An ensemble combines several models, so their individual errors partly cancel and the result is more reliable.
choice0: A model trained on several datasets at once
choice1: A model with several output columns
choice2: A model that retrains itself continuously
choice3: Several models combined so their errors partly cancel

description: What does a random forest combine?
explanation: A random forest averages the predictions of many decision trees, each trained on a different sample of the data and features.
choice0: Many decision trees trained on different samples
choice1: A decision tree and a neural network
choice2: Several datasets into one table
choice3: Many predictions from the same single tree

description: Why is a single deep decision tree prone to overfitting?
explanation: Left unrestricted it keeps splitting until it isolates individual training examples, memorising them rather than learning a pattern.
choice0: Because it ignores most of the features
choice1: Because it can keep splitting until it isolates individual training examples
choice2: Because it can only handle numeric data
choice3: Because it always uses the whole dataset at each split

description: What does the k in k-means clustering specify?
explanation: k is the number of clusters you ask the algorithm to find, chosen in advance.
choice0: The number of features to use
choice1: The number of training rounds
choice2: The number of clusters to find
choice3: The number of nearest neighbours to consider

description: What is a practical difficulty with k-means?
explanation: You must choose the number of clusters in advance, and there is no single correct answer for what it should be.
choice0: The number of clusters must be chosen in advance
choice1: It only works on labelled data
choice2: It cannot handle numeric features
choice3: It always produces exactly two clusters

description: What is a loss function?
explanation: A loss function measures how wrong the models predictions are, giving training something concrete to minimise.
choice0: The share of data lost during preparation
choice1: A measure of how wrong the predictions are, which training tries to minimise
choice2: The amount of memory training consumes
choice3: The number of examples the model misclassified

description: What does gradient descent do during training?
explanation: It repeatedly nudges the models parameters in the direction that reduces the loss.
choice0: Repeatedly adjusts parameters in the direction that reduces the loss
choice1: Removes features that contribute least
choice2: Reduces the size of the dataset step by step
choice3: Lowers the learning rate until training stops

description: What is a learning rate?
explanation: The learning rate controls how large each adjustment is during training.
choice0: How many examples are seen per second
choice1: How quickly accuracy improves per epoch
choice2: How large each adjustment to the parameters is
choice3: How often the model is evaluated

description: What tends to happen if the learning rate is far too high?
explanation: Large steps overshoot the minimum, so the loss bounces around or diverges instead of settling.
choice0: Training becomes very slow but steady
choice1: The loss bounces around or diverges instead of settling
choice2: The model automatically stops early
choice3: The model always underfits

description: What is an epoch?
explanation: One epoch is a single complete pass through the whole training set.
choice0: One prediction on the test set
choice1: One adjustment of the parameters
choice2: One fold of cross-validation
choice3: One complete pass through the training data

description: What is the purpose of regularisation?
explanation: Regularisation discourages the model from becoming too complex, trading a little training accuracy for better generalisation.
choice0: To discourage excessive complexity and improve generalisation
choice1: To speed up training
choice2: To fill in missing values
choice3: To increase the size of the training set

description: How does early stopping reduce overfitting?
explanation: Training stops once performance on held-out data stops improving, before the model starts memorising the training set.
choice0: It shortens each training step
choice1: It halts training once held-out performance stops improving
choice2: It removes the least useful features
choice3: It reduces the number of classes

description: What does dropout do in a neural network?
explanation: It randomly ignores some units during training, so the network cannot rely too heavily on any one path.
choice0: Deletes unused layers after training
choice1: Discards training examples that are too easy
choice2: Randomly ignores some units during training so no single path is over-relied on
choice3: Stops training when the loss stops falling

description: What is model drift?
explanation: The world changes, so a model trained on old patterns gradually becomes less accurate on new data.
choice0: Model accuracy decaying as the real-world patterns change
choice1: A model file being corrupted over time
choice2: Predictions arriving slower as usage grows
choice3: The training data gradually being deleted

description: Why should a deployed model be monitored rather than left alone?
explanation: Inputs and behaviour change over time, so performance can degrade silently unless it is measured continuously.
choice0: Because models consume more memory over time
choice1: Because performance can degrade silently as the data changes
choice2: Because the training data must be re-uploaded regularly
choice3: Because accuracy is only computable in production

description: What does retraining a model on recent data address?
explanation: It brings the model back in line with current patterns after drift.
choice0: Drift, by realigning the model with current patterns
choice1: Bugs in the prediction code
choice2: The need for a test set
choice3: Imbalance between the classes

description: What is transfer learning?
explanation: Transfer learning reuses a model trained on a large general task as the starting point for a related, smaller task.
choice0: Moving a model between two computers
choice1: Copying data between two projects
choice2: Converting a classifier into a regressor
choice3: Reusing a model trained on a large task as the starting point for a related one

description: Why is transfer learning attractive when you have little labelled data?
explanation: The pretrained model already encodes general patterns, so far fewer task-specific examples are needed.
choice0: The pretrained model already knows general patterns, so fewer examples are needed
choice1: It removes the need to evaluate the model
choice2: It generates additional labelled examples
choice3: It guarantees the model will not overfit

description: What is data augmentation?
explanation: Augmentation creates extra training examples by making realistic variations of existing ones, such as rotating an image.
choice0: Adding more columns to the dataset
choice1: Creating extra training examples as realistic variations of existing ones
choice2: Merging two datasets together
choice3: Increasing the number of training epochs

description: Why is a stratified split useful for imbalanced classification?
explanation: It keeps the class proportions the same in each part, so a rare class is not concentrated in one side of the split.
choice0: It preserves the class proportions in each split
choice1: It removes examples of the majority class
choice2: It sorts the data by class before splitting
choice3: It guarantees an equal number of rows per split

description: What does a ROC curve show?
explanation: It traces the trade-off between true positive rate and false positive rate as the decision threshold moves.
choice0: How the loss changes during training
choice1: The distribution of each feature
choice2: The trade-off between true and false positive rates across thresholds
choice3: How accuracy varies with dataset size

description: What does changing the decision threshold of a classifier do?
explanation: It shifts how readily the model calls something positive, moving precision and recall in opposite directions.
choice0: Trades precision against recall by changing how readily it predicts positive
choice1: Retrains the model on different data
choice2: Changes which features the model uses
choice3: Converts the model into a regressor

description: What does it mean that most models output a probability rather than a decision?
explanation: The model reports a confidence, and a threshold turns it into a yes or no, which lets you tune the trade-off afterwards.
choice0: The model is unsure and needs more training
choice1: It reports a confidence, and a threshold turns it into a decision
choice2: The output must be rounded before use
choice3: Probabilities can only be used for regression

description: Why is a simple model often the right thing to try first?
explanation: It sets a solid baseline quickly, is easy to debug and explain, and often performs close to a complex one.
choice0: It gives a fast baseline that is easy to debug and explain
choice1: Simple models never overfit
choice2: Complex models cannot be evaluated
choice3: Simple models need no test set

description: Two models score almost identically, but one is far simpler. Which should you usually prefer?
explanation: The simpler model is easier to explain, cheaper to run and less likely to be relying on a fragile quirk.
choice0: The complex one, since it will improve with more data
choice1: Whichever trained faster
choice2: The simpler one, since it is easier to explain, run and trust
choice3: Neither; always combine them
